lesson.title: Control schematics: coils, contacts and cross-references

interactive.brief: The one thing you should see is a contact, paths away from its coil, change state the moment that coil pulls in while its faint drawn copy stays put, when you press Start or Tank low.
interactive.title: The pump starter sheet, live
interactive.whatAmILookingAt: A short lesson in thirteen small screens. Some screens show an idea and the rest ask you to try it. The main picture is the control schematic of two pump starters on one sheet, drawn the IEC way. Duty pump -M1 runs on contactor -Q1, and standby pump -M2 on contactor -Q2. This sheet holds only the control circuit. The pumps and the contactors' main contacts are on the power sheet, which is not drawn. The control supply runs along the top as a line marked L, and the return along the bottom, marked N. Between them stand eight current paths, numbered 1 to 8 along the top. Path 1: level switch -B1, then the coil of level relay -K1. On this sheet -B1 is drawn open, and a tank filled above its low mark holds it closed. Path 2: Stop button -S0, normally closed, then Start 1 -S1, normally open, then a normally open contact of -K1, a normally closed contact of -Q2, the normally closed contact of overload -F1, and the coil of -Q1. Path 3: a normally open contact of -Q1, its latching contact, joined across -S1. Path 4: fed from just below -S0, Start 2 -S2, normally open, then a normally open contact of -K1, a normally closed contact of -Q1, the normally closed contact of overload -F2, and the coil of -Q2. Path 5: a normally open contact of -Q2, its latching contact, joined across -S2. Path 6: a normally open contact of -Q1 and lamp -P1, Duty running. Path 7: a normally open contact of -Q2 and lamp -P2, Standby running. Path 8: a normally closed contact of -K1 and lamp -P3, Tank low. Each coil is a rectangle with its tag beside it. Every contact carries the tag of the device that moves it. Under each coil is a small cross-reference table with two columns. The left column lists the paths of its normally open contacts, and the right one those of its normally closed ones. Under -K1 it reads 2, 4 and then 8. Under -Q1 it reads 3, 6 and then 4. Under -Q2 it reads 5, 7 and then 2. Every contact is drawn twice. A faint copy shows its drawn state, with every coil de-energised and no button pressed. Over it, in bold ink, the contact shows its present state. An energised coil is drawn bold with a soft glow. A lit lamp glows. Five buttons sit above the sheet: Start 1, Start 2, Stop, Trip -F1 and Tank low. At phone width they wrap onto two rows, with no word split. Start 1, Start 2 and Stop act while pressed and spring back. Trip -F1 opens -F1's contact until it is tapped again, as a reset. Tank low opens -B1 until it is tapped again, as the tank refilling. The rule. A coil is energised while an unbroken run of closed contacts joins it to both L and N. A normally open contact is closed while its coil is energised, and a normally closed one is open while its coil is energised. Otherwise each sits as drawn. The circuit is solved again after every press, so a latching contact holds its coil in after Start springs back. Tap any contact of -K1, -Q1 or -Q2, and its coil lights with a ring. A thin line joins the contact to the coil, and the coil's table marks the contact's path. Tap a button, -B1 or an overload contact instead, and a small card says what moves it: a hand, the tank's level, or heat from the pump's current on the power sheet. The readout Contacts not as drawn counts every contact whose present state differs from its drawn state. Buttons and switches count too. The readout Pumps running counts the energised contactors. Contacts not as drawn shows from screen 6 on. On screens 7 and 13 it reads ? until the answer is checked. It opens with the tank full, so -B1 is closed and -K1 is in. Both pumps are stopped, and Pumps running reads 0. A Sheet switch above the buttons picks IEC or US ladder. US ladder redraws the same circuit as eight horizontal rungs between two upright rails, numbered down the left. There each coil is a circle at the right end of its rung, tagged CR1 for -K1, M1 for -Q1 and M2 for -Q2. A contact is two short parallel lines, with a slash across a normally closed one, tagged with its coil's name. The overload contacts are tagged OL1 and OL2, and each lamp is a small circle with short rays. The rung numbers of each coil's contacts are written beside it, with normally closed ones marked NC. At phone width the paths are drawn tall, about 40 px apart. The coil tables sit in a row under the coils. Every tag is at least 12 px and stays readable at 360 px. Each contact is a tap target about 40 px across. Screen by screen. Screen 1, do, Still there?: the sheet as it opens. "You press Start on a DOL starter and let go. What keeps the contactor in?" Choices: The Start button stays down; A contact of the contactor itself, across Start (right); The overload's contact. Hint on The Start button stays down: "Start springs back the moment you let go. Something else carries the coil's current." Hint on The overload's contact: "The overload's contact is closed whether the contactor is in or not. Look across Start." Why: pulling in closes the contactor's own latching contact. It is wired across Start, so it keeps the coil fed after Start springs back. A right answer says "Right, you still have it." After Check, -Q1's contact in path 3 is ringed. Screen 2, show, Coils and contacts apart: the sheet as it opens. Words: "A control schematic draws a circuit as numbered current paths, from the supply at the top to the return at the bottom. Each coil sits in one path. Its contacts sit wherever they do their work. Each one carries the coil's tag." The path numbers light 1 to 8 in turn, then coil -Q1 glows with its three contacts, in paths 3, 4 and 6. Read: coil -Q1 in path 2 is picked out together with its three contacts, in paths 3, 4 and 6. Still: the end of the sweep. Screen 3, do, typed, Find the coil: the sheet as it opens, with the -Q2 contact in path 2 marked. "The contact marked in path 2 is tagged -Q2. In which path is the coil that moves it?" A typed answer: 4, a whole number. Slips: 2, "That is where the contact sits. Its coil is drawn in another path."; 1, "-K1's coil looks the same, but its tag is different. Find the coil tagged -Q2."; 5, "Path 5 holds another -Q2 contact. Find the coil itself, a rectangle." Hint: "Look along the bottom of the sheet for the coil tagged -Q2." Why: a contact belongs to the coil whose tag it carries. Coil -Q2 sits in path 4, so the contact in path 2 opens whenever -Q2 pulls in. After Check, the contact is tapped for him: coil -Q2 lights and a line joins them. Screen 4, show, The cross-reference: the sheet as it opens. Words: "Under each coil on this sheet sits its cross-reference. It lists the paths where that coil's contacts sit. Normally open ones are on the left, and normally closed ones on the right." Then "Tap any contact to find its coil." Read: tapping -K1's contact in path 8 lights coil -K1 in path 1. Its table reads 2, 4 and then 8, and marks path 8. Still: -K1's contact in path 8 tapped. Screen 5, do, typed, One coil pulls in: the sheet as it opens. "Contactor -Q1 pulls in. How many contacts on this sheet change state?" A typed answer: 3, a whole number. Slips: 2, "The contact in path 4 is normally closed. It changes too, from closed to open."; 1, "Count every path in -Q1's table, in both columns."; 4, "Start 1 springs back. Count only the contacts -Q1 moves." Hint: "Read the cross-reference under coil -Q1. Every contact it lists changes when the coil pulls in." Why: the table lists all three of -Q1's contacts on this sheet. All at once, paths 3 and 6 close and path 4 opens. After Check, Start 1 is pressed for him: -Q1 pulls in and its three contacts redraw. Screen 6, show, Drawn at rest: the sheet as it opens. Words: "Each contact on this sheet is drawn at rest, with every coil de-energised and no button pressed. Here each contact shows in bold what it is doing now. A faint copy under it shows how it is drawn. The tank is full, so -K1 is in. Its contacts already differ from the drawing." -B1 and -K1's three contacts are ringed in turn. Contacts not as drawn reads 4. Screen 7, do, Drawn closed: the sheet as it opens, with -K1's contact in path 8 marked. "-K1's contact in path 8 is drawn closed. With the tank full, is it closed now?" Choices: Yes, it is drawn closed; No, it is open (right). Hint on Yes: "The drawing shows it at rest. Is its coil at rest?" Why: the full tank holds -B1 closed, so coil -K1 is energised. A normally closed contact is open while its coil is in. So path 8 is open and the Tank low lamp is dark. After Check, path 8's contact is ringed, bold and open over its faint closed copy. Screen 8, show, Series and parallel: the sheet as it opens. Words: "Contacts one after another in a path are in series. Any one opening drops the coil out, unless another path bridges it. The latching contact in path 3 is in parallel with Start 1. It holds -Q1 in after Start springs back." Then "Press Start 1, then Trip -F1." Read: Start 1 has pulled -Q1 in, and its latching contact has held it there. Then -F1 has opened and -Q1 has dropped out. Its three contacts are back as drawn. Still: Start 1 pressed, then -F1 tripped. Screen 9, do, Start the standby: -M1 running and the tank full. "Pump -M1 runs. You press Start 2. What happens?" Choices: -M2 starts as well; Nothing happens (right); -M1 stops and -M2 starts. Hint on -M2 starts as well: "Follow path 4 from Start 2 down to coil -Q2. Is every contact closed?" Hint on -M1 stops and -M2 starts: "Start 2 sits in path 4 only. Nothing in path 2 moves when you press it." Why: -Q1 is in, so its normally closed contact in path 4 is open. Path 4 cannot reach coil -Q2, whatever Start 2 does. That is the interlock, read off the sheet. After Check, Start 2 is pressed and nothing changes. Screen 10, show, The US ladder: the sheet as it opens. Words: "A US ladder draws the same circuit sideways, as rungs between two rails. Each coil is a circle, here CR1, M1 and M2. Each contact carries its coil's tag." Then "Switch the sheet to US ladder." The IEC sheet fades out, and then the US ladder fades in. Read: the same circuit is drawn as eight rungs. Coils CR1, M1 and M2 are circles at the right, and each contact is tagged with its coil. Still: the Sheet switch on US ladder. Screen 11, do, The circle on rung 2: the US ladder, as it opens. "On the US ladder, what is the circle tagged M1 at the end of rung 2?" Choices: The duty pump's motor; The Duty running lamp; The coil of contactor -Q1 (right). Hint on The duty pump's motor: "A control sheet shows what switches the motor. The motor is on the power sheet." Hint on The Duty running lamp: "A lamp has short rays, and it sits on rung 6." Why: in the US form, a coil is drawn as a circle. M1 is the coil of -Q1, the starter for the duty pump. Its contacts on rungs 3, 4 and 6 carry the tag M1. On the IEC sheet, -M1 is the motor itself. Screen 12, do, mixed, A trip: the IEC sheet, -M1 running and the tank full. "-F1 trips while -M1 runs. Which pump can you start now?" Choices: Neither; Only -M1; Only -M2 (right); Both. Hint on Neither: "-Q1 has dropped out, so its contact in path 4 has closed again." Hint on Only -M1: "-F1's contact is in -Q1's own path, and it stays open until it is reset." Hint on Both: "-M2 can start now. Can path 2 reach coil -Q1 with -F1 open?" Why: -F1 opening breaks path 2, so -Q1 drops out. Its normally closed contact in path 4 closes again. Now path 4 waits only for Start 2. -M1 cannot restart until -F1 is reset. After Check, -F1 trips, Start 2 is pressed for him and -M2 runs. Screen 13, do, mixed, typed, Not as drawn: the IEC sheet, -M1 running and the tank full. "Pump -M1 runs with the tank full. How many contacts on the sheet are not in their drawn state?" A typed answer: 7, a whole number. Slips: 6, "-B1 counts too. It is drawn open, and the full tank holds it closed."; 4, "-Q1 is in, and all three of its contacts have changed."; 3, "Two coils are in, -K1 and -Q1. Count both tables, and -B1."; 8, "Stop -S0 is drawn closed, and it is closed now. It changes only while pressed." Hint: "Count -B1, then every contact in the table of each coil that is in." Why: -B1 is closed, though drawn open. -K1 and -Q1 are both in, and each has three contacts on this sheet. So 1 + 3 + 3 makes 7 contacts not as drawn. Contacts not as drawn shows 7 once the answer is checked.
interactive.ignores: The sheet has far fewer parts than a real starter panel, and only the control circuit is drawn. A contact here changes the instant its coil pulls in or drops out, with no bounce or delay. The overload trips from a button, not from heat, and the level switch opens from a button, not a float. Drawing -B1 open is this example's choice. The cross-reference table is one simple layout. Real sheets set it out in several ways. They often point to contacts on other sheets by sheet and path. The tags are names on this sheet only. Their letters also carry meanings in the standards, which are left out here.

explain.text:
A control schematic draws each coil in one place. It draws each of the coil's contacts where that contact does its work. A contact belongs to the coil whose tag it carries, however far apart the two are drawn. So you find a contact's coil by its tag, and a coil's contacts by the coil's [[cross-reference]].

The sheet draws the circuit as [[current path]]s. Each one is a line from the control supply at the top to the return at the bottom. The paths are numbered along the top. A coil is energised while an unbroken run of closed contacts joins it to both lines. Each coil usually sits in its own path, and each contact is drawn in the path it switches. That way each path reads top to bottom as one circuit, with most of what can stop its coil in it. Check the line that feeds it too. Stop -S0 in path 2 also feeds path 4. On the example sheet, coil -Q1 sits in path 2. Its latching contact is in path 3, and its run lamp's contact in path 6. A contact that blocks the standby pump sits in path 4.

A coil's contacts can even sit on another sheet. You match them by tag and by the cross-reference, never by how alike two coils look.[^1] On this sheet the cross-reference is a short table of paths under each coil. It lists normally open contacts first, then normally closed. Under -Q1 it reads 3 and 6, then 4. When -Q1 pulls in, all three change over. Paths 3 and 6 close, and path 4 opens.

A US ladder draws the same circuit sideways, in rungs. Each coil is a circle, and each contact carries its coil's tag. There, M1 is the coil of -Q1. On the IEC sheet, -M1 is the motor itself.

Unless the sheet says otherwise, each contact is shown in its drawn state. That means its coil is de-energised and no button is pressed. So a normally closed contact is drawn closed even while its coil is energised and the contact is open.[^2] On the example sheet, a full tank holds level switch -B1 closed, so relay -K1 is in. Its normally closed contact in path 8 is drawn closed, but it is open. So the Tank low lamp is dark. To know what a contact is doing now, find its coil and ask whether that coil is in. Then each path reads as series and parallel, like any circuit you know. A contact in series that opens on an unsafe condition is called a [[permissive]].[^3] The -K1 contacts in paths 2 and 4 are permissives. A low tank opens them, so neither pump can run.

**A contact belongs to the coil whose tag it carries, wherever it is drawn, and it is usually drawn at rest, so its coil tells you what it is doing now.**

analogy.text: You know this from a lighting contactor in a distribution board, switched by a time switch or a photocell. Its coil is wired from the control side. Its main contacts switch circuits that may run to the far end of the building. You find which circuits it switches by its label and the circuit chart, never by where the lights are. A control schematic works the same way. Each contact belongs to the coil whose tag it carries.
analogy.breaks: In a board, the coil and its contacts sit in one box you can see. On a schematic they can be paths or sheets apart. Only the tag and the cross-reference join them. And the schematic usually shows every contact at rest, not as the time switch has it now.

practice.text:
- Isolate, lock off and prove dead as you always do. A schematic shows how a circuit works, never that it is dead.
- Find where the sheet's supply lines come from. A control circuit can be fed from somewhere other than the motor's own feed.
- For a contact you are puzzling over, read its tag, then find the coil with that tag. Never go by the nearest coil, or one that looks the same.
- For a coil, read its cross-reference. Visit every path it lists, in both columns.
- Remember each contact is drawn at rest, unless the sheet says otherwise. For each one, ask whether its coil is in now. If it is, the contact has changed over.
- Then read each path as series and parallel. Contacts in series must all be closed for the coil to pull in. The coil's own contact across Start holds it in after Start springs back.
- In the panel, check that each device carries the tag the sheet gives it.

**Rule of thumb:** a contact does what its own coil tells it, not what its neighbours on the sheet do.

**Worked example:** why won't standby pump -M2 start while -M1 runs? Coil -Q2 sits in path 4, so every contact in path 4 must be closed for it to pull in. Path 4 holds a normally closed contact tagged -Q1. -M1 runs, so coil -Q1 is in, and that contact is open. That is the interlock doing its job. Stop -M1, and -Q2 can pull in.

**Common mistakes**
- Looking for a coil's contacts next to it. They sit wherever they do their work.
- Matching a contact to the nearest coil, or to one that looks the same, instead of by its tag.
- Reading the drawing as the plant's present state. It shows the contacts at rest.
- Forgetting the normally closed contacts. When a coil pulls in, they open.
- Taking a US coil, a circle, for the motor or a lamp.

interactive.html:
The control circuit of two example pump starters, duty and standby, drawn on one sheet in eight numbered current paths. Duty pump -M1 runs on contactor -Q1, and standby pump -M2 on -Q2. The pumps are on the power sheet.

An example sheet, far simpler than a real starter panel. A bold line is joined to the supply, L.
interactive.title: The pump starter sheet, live
interactive.brief: The one thing you should see is a contact, paths away from its coil, change state the moment that coil pulls in while its faint drawn copy stays put, when you press Start or Tank low.

checks.label: Opening with the tank full: -B1 is closed, so -K1 is in and both pumps are stopped. -B1 and the three contacts of -K1 are not as drawn, which makes 4, and 0 pumps run
Each coil's table lists the paths of its contacts, normally open on the left: -K1 2, 4 then 8; -Q1 3, 6 then 4; -Q2 5, 7 then 2

Start 1 pressed and let go: -Q1 stays in through its latching contact in path 3. Stop drops it out. With -F1 tripped, or the tank low, Start 1 cannot pull it in, and the tank going low stops a running pump
The interlock: with -Q1 in, Start 2 changes nothing. Once -F1 trips, -Q1 drops out and Start 2 starts the standby pump. With -Q2 in, Start 1 changes nothing

Worked by hand: the -Q2 contact in path 2 has its coil in path 4 (slips 2, 1 and 5); -Q1 pulling in changes 3 contacts (slips 2, 1 and 4); with the duty pump running, 7 contacts are not as drawn (slips 6, 4, 3 and 8); the typed fields ask exactly these
A normally closed contact is drawn closed even if its coil is energised and the contact is open: -K1's contact in path 8 is drawn closed, and with the tank full it is open

A coil and its contacts may sit in different rungs, matched by reference designation and cross-reference: every contact of -K1, -Q1 and -Q2 sits in another path from its coil, and its path is in that coil's table

Before an answer nothing gives it away: each puzzle opens with nothing picked out but its marked contact, Contacts not as drawn is hidden before screen 6, and the two drawn-state puzzles show every contact as drawn with that readout as ?
Every demonstration settles within 4.5 s of its screen opening, and every answer's motion within 3 s

applied.problem: On this sheet Stop -S0 sits in path 2 yet also stops -Q2 in path 4, so a path does not hold everything that can stop its coil. Real contacts need not change at one instant, and the bold line drops the rule that a sheet can say it is drawn otherwise.

"A contact across a button holds the coil in" is too general: only the coil's own normally open contact across Start latches it, and only while the rest of its path is closed; another contact across a button, say across Stop, would do something else entirely.
Screen 8 says any one contact in series opening drops the coil out, but on this sheet Start 1 is in series in path 2 and opening it does not drop -Q1 out, because the latch in path 3 bridges it.
"The schematic shows every contact at rest" is stated without the exception the explanation and practice keep: a sheet can say it is drawn in another state, which lesson i9 teaches Dan to check.
